name: Progressive lenses

lead: Progressive lenses are glasses lenses whose power changes gradually from the distance prescription at the top to the reading power at the bottom. Because there is no visible line, as there is in a traditional bifocal, the lenses look like ordinary single-vision glasses.

For appearance, that means people who need reading correction can wear glasses without the line that is often read as a sign of age. They were developed mainly as a vision correction, and the cosmetic benefit is a side effect of that design.

paras: An optician measures the pupil position and frame fit and orders lenses with a chosen reading addition. Wearers look through the top for distance, the middle for arm's-length tasks and the bottom for reading. Adjustment typically takes from a few hours to about two weeks, according to Wikipedia's summary of the topic.

Edges of the lens have blur and distortion, which can cause headaches or dizziness while adapting, and a minority of wearers never adapt. Poor measurement of pupil height or distance can reduce comfort. They generally cost more than bifocals or single-vision lenses.

Reading correction without a visible bifocal line
angle.text: Progressives let people who need reading correction wear glasses without a visible bifocal line. Users choose them for the cleaner lens appearance as well as for seamless focus from far to near.

lead: Progressive lenses, also called progressive addition lenses or varifocals, are eyeglass lenses for presbyopia, the age-related loss of near focusing. Their power increases smoothly from the distance prescription at the top to the full reading addition at the bottom.[1][2]

The look-related appeal is that they have no visible lines. Where bifocals and trifocals show a clear dividing line, progressives resemble ordinary single-vision lenses and so avoid the line that is commonly associated with ageing.[2] A 1983 clinical study compared acceptance of a progressive lens with a blended bifocal, another form of "invisible" addition lens.[3]

Research on the lenses covers optical design, fitting and adaptation. Reviews trace six decades of design work and the move to free-form surfacing and wavefront technology,[1][4] and a nationwide clinical trial examined how well a broad range of patients adapted to a variable-design progressive.[5]

paras: Presbyopia is defined as the point at which the normal age-related narrowing of the eye's focusing range leaves near vision insufficient even with the best distance correction.[6] Progressives address it with a lens surface whose power rises gradually along a corridor, with the reading addition typically ranging from 0.75 to 3.50 diopters.[2]
Designs have developed from conventional surfaces to free-form manufacturing and wavefront-based optimisation.[1][4]

Owen Aves patented an early design in 1907 and a commercial progressive was reportedly sold in 1922; modern designs trace to Bernard Maitenaz's Varilux, patented in 1953 and sold from 1959, with an aspheric version in 1972. Zeiss introduced free-form manufacturing in 1983.[2]

Fitting requires correct positioning of the lens relative to the pupil. A review in Survey of Ophthalmology discusses vertical and horizontal positioning of multifocal and progressive lenses, noting that fitting variables can lead to patient dissatisfaction.[7] A theoretical study examined how poorly measured individual parameters affect performance.[8]
Wearers may notice peripheral blur and a period of adjustment; manufacturers report acceptance of 90 to 98 percent.[2]

A 1983 double-masked comparison studied acceptance of progressive and blended bifocal lenses.[3] A nationwide clinical trial reported on the adaptability of randomly selected patients to a variable-design progressive.[5] In children, progressive lenses have been studied for slowing myopia; a 2012 review concluded the average effect was small, with larger effects in children with particular binocular features.[9] The Hong Kong progressive lens myopia control study is one such trial.[10]

timeline.event: Owen Aves patents an early progressive design.[2]
